works_at.note: data/structures/chicago_democrat_office.json is recorded as a printing office AND a store on exactly this reading: the paper's imprint and Kimball's advertisement put both at the corner of South Water and Clark in the same issue. Inferred rather than documented because 'on the corner of' names a junction and not a building, and two businesses at one junction need not share one roof.

present_on_scene_date.note: Documented at the junction in November 1833; a W. Kimball is a town trustee in July 1835 and may or may not be the same man.

persons.name: W. Kimball

occupation.note: His own signed advertisement for a 'New Store' at the corner of South Water and Clark, offering dry goods, crockery, hardware, cutlery, caps and cloth, in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833.

persons.note: A SECOND, INDEPENDENTLY ATTESTED OCCUPANT OF THE DEMOCRAT'S OWN JUNCTION in the same issue of the same paper - which is why this project reads the printing office and the new store as sharing a building. Andreas's 1835 town officers list has a 'W. Kimball' among the nine trustees elected at the third town election of July 1835, and if that is this man he holds office on or about the scene date. THE IDENTIFICATION IS NOT MADE HERE: the surname is common in this record, and this project already keeps a separate Kimball (Dr E. S. Kimberly's partner is Pruyne, but a druggist 'Kimball & Porter' occupied the same corner later, and Andreas spells both Kimball and Kimberly loosely). The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Kimball, Walter, 291 Oak street, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS2A — one bearer of the surname, the forename initial agrees, and the resident's own record spells the roster's forename 'walter' — the discriminator the roster's initials do not supply (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json).

resident_research.evidence_for: The project's 26 November 1833 Chicago Democrat source records W. Kimball's New Store at the South Water/Clark junction. The unusual initial-plus-surname form matches the resident record and strengthens the merchant identity, but does not safely expand the initial or prove scene-date occupancy.

This household exists mainly to make the reasoning behind chicago_democrat_office visible as a person rather than as a paragraph: two named businesses, one junction, one building in the model, one inference holding them together.
